10480:
Medieval is an adjective that means relating to or characteristic of the Middle Ages — a long period in European history that lasted roughly from the 5th century AD to the late 15th century AD (approximately 400 AD to 1500 AD).

So whenever you call something "medieval," you are saying it belongs to, comes from, or is typical of that specific era of history.

To really understand the word, you need a mental picture of the period it refers to.

The Middle Ages is the name historians gave to the centuries that fell between two great eras: the ancient world (the age of the Greek and Roman empires) and the modern world (the Renaissance and beyond). It was the long in-between period — hence the word "middle." It was dominated by the Catholic Church, feudal kingdoms, castles, knights, and a way of life very different from what we know today.

Civilisation during this time was mostly agricultural, largely illiterate, governed by kings and nobles, shaped heavily by religion, and marked by things like the Black Plague, the Crusades, and constant warfare between kingdoms.
What kinds of things can be described as "medieval"?

The adjective can be applied to almost anything that has a connection to that era:

Architecture and places — A stone castle with towers and a drawbridge is medieval architecture. The great Gothic cathedrals of Europe (like Notre-Dame in Paris) are medieval buildings. A walled city from that period is a medieval town.

People and roles — A knight in armour is a medieval warrior. A monk copying manuscripts by candlelight in a monastery is a medieval scholar. A king ruling over lords and peasants is a medieval ruler.

Society and systems — The feudal system — where peasants worked land owned by lords, who in turn served a king — is a medieval social structure. The practice of arranged marriages based on land and power, or the idea that women had very few rights, are medieval social norms.

Art, literature, and culture — Illuminated manuscripts (hand-drawn and decorated religious texts), Gregorian chants, tales of King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table — these are all medieval art and culture.

Warfare and weapons — Swords, lances, bows and arrows, catapults, siege warfare — these are medieval weapons and fighting methods. The image of two armies of armoured knights clashing on a battlefield is essentially a medieval scene.

Medicine and science — Medieval medicine was based on superstition, religious belief, and ancient Greek theories rather than scientific evidence. Bloodletting (cutting a patient to drain "bad blood") and herbs were common medieval treatments.

Law and punishment — Trials by ordeal (where guilt or innocence was decided by, say, holding a hot iron — if your hand healed, you were innocent), public executions, and torture were medieval forms of justice.

Here is where the word becomes even more interesting. In everyday modern usage, medieval is often used figuratively — not literally about the Middle Ages, but as a way of calling something brutally harsh, outrageously cruel, excessively primitive, or shockingly outdated.

This usage exists because the Middle Ages have a reputation (somewhat exaggerated, but not entirely untrue) for being a time of cruelty, ignorance, and barbarism.

Examples:

  • "The conditions in that prison are absolutely medieval." → The conditions are inhumanly harsh and primitive, like something from a dark era.
  • "Their disciplinary methods are medieval." → Their punishments are cruel and backwards.
  • "Don't get medieval on me!" → Don't be excessively brutal or harsh.
  • "That hospital equipment looks medieval." → It looks ancient, outdated, and primitive.

In all these cases, the speaker is not literally talking about the 5th–15th centuries. They are using "medieval" as a powerful way to say: this is backwards, brutal, or shockingly out of place in the modern world.

It is mostly a European term. "Medieval" technically refers to European history. Other civilisations — the Islamic Golden Age, Song Dynasty China, the Mughal precursors in India — were flourishing at the same time, often more advanced than Europe. So saying medieval China or medieval India is slightly loose usage; historians prefer terms like "classical" or specific dynasty names for those regions. However, "medieval" is sometimes used loosely for other regions to mean "the equivalent period in history."

It is not always negative. In historical contexts, "medieval" is completely neutral — it simply labels a time period. You can admire medieval architecture, love medieval literature, or study medieval philosophy without any negative implication. The negative connotation only kicks in when the word is used figuratively in modern speech.

It is often romanticised too. Popular culture (fantasy films, books, games) tends to romanticise the Middle Ages — castles, dragons, chivalry, magic. When people say something has a "medieval feel" about a fantasy story or game, they mean it has that romantic, mythic, old-world flavour.

The degree it covers is wide. The Middle Ages span about a thousand years (roughly 500 AD–1500 AD), which is enormous. Historians even divide it into the Early Middle Ages, the High Middle Ages, and the Late Middle Ages. So "medieval" covers a huge sweep of time, and life in 600 AD was very different from life in 1400 AD — yet both are correctly called medieval.

Medieval (adjective) has two related uses:

  1. Historical and literal — "of or relating to the Middle Ages" (roughly 400–1500 AD in Europe): medieval castles, medieval warfare, medieval society.
  2. Figurative and informal — "brutally harsh, primitive, or shockingly outdated": "Those working conditions are absolutely medieval."

The word carries a strong visual and emotional charge. When you hear it, think: stone castles, iron swords, feudal lords, devout faith, rough living, and a world without science or modern rights — and you will always use and understand it correctly.
10481:
Mediocre means just average — not good, not bad, but sitting uncomfortably in the middle. It describes something (or someone) that is neither impressive nor terrible. It is ordinary in a disappointing way.

Think of a scale from 1 to 10. Excellent things sit at 8, 9, or 10. Truly bad things sit at 1 or 2. Mediocre things sit around 4, 5, or 6 — the middle zone where nothing is really wrong, but nothing is really right either.
The Key Feeling Behind the Word

Here is the most important thing to understand: mediocre is not a neutral word. Even though it describes the middle of the scale, it feels negative when you use it. Why? Because when we call something mediocre, we are implying that it could — and should — have been better. It suggests a kind of quiet disappointment.

Imagine you go to a restaurant for the first time and you say: "The food was mediocre." You are not saying the food made you sick. You are saying it was dull, unremarkable, and forgettable. You expected more. That feeling — of expecting more and getting just enough — is at the heart of mediocre.

It helps to understand what mediocre is not, so you don't confuse it with similar words:

  • Mediocre ≠ Terrible. Terrible means genuinely bad. Mediocre is not that low. A mediocre student still passes their exams — they just never stand out.
  • Mediocre ≠ Okay or acceptable. In everyday speech, when people say "it was okay," they might mean they are fine with it. But mediocre carries a slight sting — it suggests the person is not fully fine with it.
  • Mediocre ≠ Average in a purely mathematical sense. In math, "average" is a neutral calculation. But mediocre is a judgment — it carries a tone of mild criticism or disappointment.

Mediocre can describe almost anything — a person's skill, a movie, a performance, a meal, a product, a result, or even an era of time.

Here are some natural examples:

  • "It was a mediocre film — the story was predictable and the acting was flat."
  • "He is a mediocre programmer. He can get basic tasks done, but struggles with anything complex."
  • "I had high hopes for that restaurant, but the experience was mediocre at best."
  • "She refused to settle for a mediocre life — she wanted to achieve something meaningful."
  • "The team delivered a mediocre performance in the first half of the match."

Notice that in all these cases, the thing being described is not a disaster — it is just not good enough.

You will often see mediocre paired with the phrase "at best," as in: "The results were mediocre at best." This phrase makes the criticism even stronger. It means: "Even if I am being generous and looking at this in the best possible light, the highest I can rate it is mediocre." It is a polite but cutting way to criticize something.

Mediocre has a small range within itself:

  • Borderline mediocre — almost acceptable, nearly reaching the point where you would not complain.
  • Solidly mediocre — undeniably average, nothing worth noting positively.
  • Deeply mediocre — still not the worst, but so consistently average across every aspect that the word starts to feel almost insulting.

When mediocre is used to describe a person, it refers specifically to their ability, effort, or output — not their character or personality. To call someone mediocre is to say they perform at an average or below-expected level in a particular area.

  • "A mediocre teacher" = a teacher who gets through lessons but does not truly inspire, challenge, or connect with students.
  • "A mediocre athlete" = an athlete who participates and competes, but rarely wins or impresses.

Importantly, calling someone mediocre is considered mildly insulting in most social contexts, so this word is used carefully in polite conversation. It is more commonly used to describe things than people, unless the speaker is being deliberately critical.

Words that mean the opposite of mediocre include: exceptional, outstanding, excellent, superior, remarkable, distinguished, and first-rate. These all point to the high end of the quality scale — exactly where mediocre is not.
Mediocre means disappointingly average — good enough to function, but not good enough to impress, remember, or feel proud of.
10482:
Mediocrity means the quality or state of being just okay — not bad enough to fail, but not good enough to impress. It lives right in the middle: below excellence, above failure. Think of a scale from 1 to 10. Mediocrity sits around a 5 — technically passing, but nothing to be proud of.

The word is almost always used as a criticism. When someone calls a thing mediocre, they're not being neutral — they're expressing disappointment, often because they expected or hoped for something better.

Here's what makes mediocrity different from just being "average": it carries a sense of wasted potential. It suggests that something — or someone — could have been much better, but settled for the middle ground instead.

Imagine a student who is clearly intelligent but turns in lazy, half-effort work that barely meets requirements. That work is mediocre. It's not wrong exactly, but it's flat, uninspired, and forgettable. That flatness is the heart of mediocrity.

It helps to know what this word does not mean, because learners sometimes confuse it with related ideas.

Mediocrity is not failure. A failure falls short — it doesn't work, it collapses, it disappoints in an obvious way. Mediocrity, on the other hand, technically functions — it just doesn't do anything remarkable. A restaurant that gives you food that's edible but bland and forgettable isn't a failure — it's mediocre.

Mediocrity is not the same as "average" in a purely mathematical sense. In math or statistics, "average" is neutral — it's just the middle value with no judgment attached. But "mediocrity" always carries a judgment. It says: this should have been better.

Mediocrity is not necessarily an accident. It can also be the result of complacency — a choice (conscious or not) to stop pushing, to do the bare minimum, to coast.

Mediocrity is a flexible word. It can describe:

A piece of work — a painting, a book, a film, a meal, a report. "The screenplay was filled with mediocrity — predictable dialogue, no surprises, nothing that made you feel anything."

A performance — in sports, arts, academics, or business. "After three seasons of mediocrity, the football team finally hired a coach who demanded excellence."

A person — though this is harsher. When used about a person, it usually means they lack ambition, talent, or drive. "He was talented early in his career, but he eventually became just another mediocrity in a crowded industry."

A system, institution, or culture — "A culture of mediocrity had settled into the company — nobody tried to do more than what was asked of them."

The plural is mediocrities, and it has two uses:

Referring to multiple mediocre things: "The gallery was full of mediocrities — paintings so ordinary you forgot them as soon as you turned away."

Referring to mediocre people: "The truly talented were surrounded by mediocrities who had gotten ahead through connections, not skill."

"Settle for mediocrity" — to accept an average result when you could have pushed for something better. "She was too ambitious to settle for mediocrity in her career."

"Rise above mediocrity" — to exceed ordinary, average standards. "The film rises above mediocrity thanks to an extraordinary lead performance."

"Sink into mediocrity" — to gradually fall from a higher standard to a disappointing average. "The once-great band sank into mediocrity after losing their best songwriter."

"A culture of mediocrity" — an environment where average effort and average results have become the accepted norm.

Words that are close in meaning to mediocrity: ordinariness, averageness, unremarkableness, adequacy, dullness.

Words that are the opposite of mediocrity: excellence, brilliance, mastery, distinction, superiority, greatness.
The Tone and Attitude of the Word

Mediocrity is a word with weight to it. When someone uses it, they're not just describing — they're evaluating, and the evaluation is unflattering. It is the language of people who have standards, who believe things should be excellent, and who are frustrated when they are not.

It is also often used in motivational or philosophical contexts. Many thinkers, leaders, coaches, and artists use the word to warn against complacency — the dangerous comfort of being "good enough." The idea is that mediocrity is not a safe middle ground; it's a quiet trap.
One Final Way to Remember It

Think of mediocrity as the land of the forgettable. Truly bad things are remembered — they shock or offend. Truly great things are remembered — they inspire or move you. Mediocre things? They vanish from your memory the moment they're over. That invisible, forgettable, "meh" quality — that is mediocrity.
10483:
To meditate means to engage your mind in a slow, deliberate, and focused way — either inward (on your own mental state) or outward (on a topic or idea). The word carries a sense of intentional stillness and purposeful depth. You are not just thinking; you are thinking in a particular way — carefully, quietly, and without rushing.

The verb has two main senses, and understanding both will give you complete command of the word.

This is the sense you will encounter most often in modern life.

To meditate means to engage in the mental and spiritual practice of turning your attention inward, calming the mind, and resting in a state of focused awareness. A person who meditates typically sits quietly, closes their eyes, and directs their attention to something specific — most commonly their own breathing — while allowing other thoughts to pass by without chasing them.

The goal is not to empty the mind entirely (which is a common myth), but rather to observe the mind without being swept away by it. You notice a thought, let it go, and gently bring your focus back to the anchor — the breath, a sound, a repeated word (called a mantra), or simply the present moment.

Examples:

  • She meditates for twenty minutes every morning before work.
  • He has been meditating regularly since he discovered mindfulness three years ago.
  • I find it difficult to meditate when there is noise around me.
  • They meditated together in silence for half an hour.

When used this way, "meditate" is almost always used without an object — you simply meditate. You don't meditate something; you just meditate. (The object, if any, usually follows "on" — which belongs to Sense 2 below.)

The practice itself can vary widely — from Buddhist meditation, to yoga-based meditation, to modern secular mindfulness — but the verb covers all of these forms.
Sense 2: To Think Deeply and Carefully About Something

This is the older, more formal sense of the word, and it is still very much alive in modern English, especially in writing and serious speech.

To meditate on/upon something means to think about it slowly, deeply, and at length — to dwell on it thoughtfully, to turn it over in your mind with full attention. It is much stronger than simply "thinking about" something. It implies that you are giving something your full, unhurried, serious mental attention — as if you are sitting with an idea and really living inside it for a while.

This sense always requires the preposition "on" or "upon" to connect the verb to its object.

Examples:

  • She meditated on what he had said to her, long after he had gone.
  • The philosopher spent years meditating on the nature of time.
  • He sat by the river and meditated upon the meaning of loss.
  • Before giving his answer, he meditated on all the possible consequences.

Notice the quality of attention here — it is not a quick, passing thought. To meditate on something is to give it the kind of slow, absorbed, and deeply serious thought that one might give to a life-changing decision, a profound question, or a painful experience.
Sense 3: To Plan or Intend (Formal / Literary)

There is a third, less common sense — mostly found in older literature or very formal writing — where "meditate" means to plan or have in mind to do something, particularly something serious or significant.

Examples:

  • He meditated revenge against those who had wronged him.
  • She was meditating a complete change of career.

In this sense, the verb takes a direct object (revenge, a plan, a course of action) without needing "on." It suggests that someone is not only thinking about something but is seriously forming an intention to do it. You will not encounter this sense in everyday conversation, but you may come across it in literature or formal prose.
How the Senses Relate to Each Other

All three senses share a common thread: deliberate, deep, inward-turned mental activity. Whether you are meditating (sitting in stillness and awareness), meditating on a question (thinking about it with full seriousness), or meditating a plan (privately forming an intention), the word always implies that the mind is engaged in a slow, purposeful, and concentrated way — the opposite of distraction, rushing, or casual thought.

Meditate (no object) → the practice of meditation
She meditates daily.

Meditate on / upon something → to think deeply about something
He meditated on her words.

Meditate something (formal/literary) → to plan or intend
She meditated a response.

Common collocations:

  • meditate regularly / daily
  • meditate on a problem / question / idea / meaning / life
  • meditate in silence / stillness
  • sit and meditate
  • meditate upon one's actions (reflecting on what you have done)
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Sense 1 (the practice) is completely common and everyday — you will hear it in casual conversation, health and wellness contexts, apps, and news articles without any formality.

Sense 2 (to think deeply) is slightly more formal or literary, but not so much that it sounds out of place in ordinary educated speech or writing. It carries a quiet, serious tone — it elevates what you are describing beyond mere thinking.

Sense 3 (to intend/plan) is distinctly literary and formal, rarely heard in spoken conversation today.

When "meditate" is used in Sense 1, it often carries a connotation of regularity and discipline — people meditate as a practice they return to, not just something they did once. Saying "I meditate" implies a habit more than a one-time action.

In Sense 2, there is a richness to the word that plain alternatives like "think about" or "consider" do not fully capture. If someone says "I have been meditating on this question," it tells you not just that they thought about it, but that they gave it serious, sustained, private attention — the kind that happens in quiet moments, perhaps over days or weeks.
10484: Meditation means the act of giving your full, focused attention to something — either inward (your own mind) or to a subject you're thinking deeply about. It is always a deliberate, intentional mental act. You choose to do it. It doesn't happen accidentally.

The word "meditation" carries a few distinct but related meanings depending on the context it appears in.

Meaning 1: A Mental Practice for Stillness and Awareness

This is the most widely known meaning today. Meditation here refers to a deliberate practice in which a person trains their mind to focus, calm down, or become deeply aware of the present moment. The person usually sits quietly, closes their eyes, and directs their attention to something specific — such as their own breathing, a repeated word or sound, or the sensations in their body — while gently letting go of distracting thoughts.

The goal isn't to stop thinking entirely (which is a common misunderstanding). The goal is to observe your own mind without being swept away by it. You notice a thought, acknowledge it, and return your focus to your chosen point of attention. Over and over again. That returning of focus is the practice.

People practise meditation for many reasons: to reduce stress, to develop emotional calmness, to improve concentration, to understand themselves better, or as part of a spiritual or religious life.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "She began daily meditation to help manage her anxiety."
  • "After twenty minutes of meditation, he felt a deep sense of peace."
  • "Meditation has been shown to reduce stress levels."

Meaning 2: A Period of Quiet, Deep Thought

In a broader and older sense, meditation simply means serious, careful, sustained thinking about something. It doesn't involve any special technique. It just means you are sitting with a thought — turning it over slowly in your mind, examining it from different angles, without rushing to a conclusion.

In this sense, meditation is the opposite of quick, scattered, or distracted thinking. It is slow, intentional, and deep.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "Lost in meditation, she didn't hear him enter the room."
  • "He spent the evening in quiet meditation on the choices he had made."

Meaning 3: A Piece of Reflective Writing or Speech

When used in a literary or intellectual context, a "meditation" is a written or spoken work in which someone thinks deeply and reflectively about a particular subject. It is not an argument trying to prove a point, and it is not a simple description of facts. It is more like the author thinking out loud on the page — exploring, questioning, and reflecting.

A meditation of this kind tends to be personal, thoughtful, and philosophical in tone.

Examples in a sentence:

  • "His short book is a meditation on loss and memory."
  • "The poem reads as a meditation on the passage of time."
  • "She delivered a quiet meditation on what it means to forgive."

Even though these three meanings appear in different contexts, they share the same underlying quality: deliberate, focused, inward attention. Whether you are practising a breathing technique, sitting alone thinking about a difficult decision, or writing a reflective essay — in each case, you are turning your attention deliberately inward or deeply toward something, without distraction and without hurry. That quality is what makes all three uses of the word "meditation" belong to the same family.

• It is not daydreaming. Daydreaming is passive and wandering. Meditation is intentional and directed.
  • It is not sleep. Meditation involves alert, wakeful awareness — even when the body is still and relaxed.
  • It is not thinking hard to solve a problem (like doing math in your head). Meditation is more about observing and being present than about calculating or problem-solving.
  • It is not exclusively religious. While meditation has deep roots in traditions like Buddhism, Hinduism, and Christianity, it is also practised today in entirely secular (non-religious) settings — in hospitals, schools, workplaces, and clinics.

• "In deep meditation" — fully absorbed in the mental practice or in serious thought.
  • "A meditation on something" — a reflective piece of writing or speech about that subject.
  • "Guided meditation" — a form of the practice where a teacher or recording leads you through the experience step by step.
  • "Mindfulness meditation" — a specific type of the practice focused on paying attention to the present moment, non-judgmentally.
  • "Fall into / enter meditation" — to begin or settle into the practice or state of meditation.

Meditation (noun) is the deliberate act of focusing the mind — whether as a disciplined mental practice for calm and self-awareness, as a period of serious personal reflection, or as a thoughtful piece of writing that explores an idea deeply — and in every case it is intentional, inward, and unhurried.
10485:
Meditative describes anything that has the quality of deep, calm, quiet reflection — a quality of being absorbed in thought, turned inward, still, and unhurried.

Think of someone sitting alone, eyes soft, completely absorbed in their own thoughts — not anxious, not distracted, just quietly and deeply thinking. That state, and anything that resembles or evokes that state, is meditative.

The adjective is flexible. It can describe a person, an activity, a mood, a piece of writing, music, a place, or even a look on someone's face.

A person or their expression:
When someone looks meditative, they appear to be absorbed in deep, quiet thought. Their mind is focused inward. They are not chatting, not reacting to the world around them — they seem to have retreated into their own interior world, calmly.

"She sat by the window with a meditative expression, barely noticing the rain."

An activity:
An activity is meditative when it is done slowly, quietly, and with calm, focused attention — in a way that turns the mind inward or allows deep thought. It doesn't have to be actual meditation. A long walk, gardening, knitting, or even washing dishes can be meditative if they are done in that spirit.

"He found chopping vegetables meditative — the rhythm of it cleared his mind."

A piece of music, art, or writing:
Music, poetry, paintings, or prose can be called meditative when they create a mood of quiet depth, stillness, and contemplation — when they slow you down and draw you inward rather than exciting or distracting you.

"The piece is slow and meditative, asking the listener to be still and simply feel."

"Her essays are meditative rather than argumentative — she doesn't rush to conclusions; she wanders through ideas slowly and deeply."

A place or atmosphere:
A place is meditative when it feels calm, still, and conducive to deep thought — when simply being there makes you quiet inside.

"The monastery had a meditative quality — the stone walls, the silence, the slow movement of the monks."
The Feeling at the Centre of the Word

No matter what it describes, the word always carries the same cluster of qualities:

  • Calm — not agitated or restless
  • Deep — not shallow or surface-level
  • Inward — turned toward one's inner world, not outward toward noise and distraction
  • Unhurried — slow, patient, without urgency
  • Focused — absorbed, not scattered

If something has all of these qualities, or strongly evokes them, it is meditative.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close cousins, and understanding the differences will sharpen your sense of meditative precisely.

Thoughtful — the most general of these. It just means "involving thought" or "thinking carefully." A thoughtful person considers things carefully. But thoughtful doesn't carry the sense of calm depth, stillness, or inward focus that meditative does. You can be thoughtful in a busy, practical way. Meditative always implies a quality of quiet, absorbed depth.

Pensive — means deep in thought, but with an emotional weight. A pensive person seems to be mulling over something troubling, uncertain, or slightly sad. Meditative is more neutral and peaceful — it doesn't carry that note of worry or sadness.

Reflective — close to meditative, but reflective specifically implies looking back — thinking about the past, considering what has already happened. Meditative is broader: it doesn't require looking back. You can be meditative while contemplating the present moment, or thinking about nothing in particular.

Contemplative — very close to meditative, and often interchangeable. If there is a subtle difference: contemplative leans slightly toward observing something carefully (you contemplate an object, an idea, a scene). Meditative leans slightly more toward an inner state of being — the quality of calm, absorbed stillness itself. In practice, both words are used in very similar ways.
A Few More Examples to Lock It In

"The yoga session ended with a meditative silence."

(The silence had the quality of deep, still, inward calm.)

"He spoke in a slow, meditative tone, as if thinking out loud."

(His manner of speaking was unhurried, deeply thoughtful, absorbed.)

"The landscape has something meditative about it — flat, quiet, endless."

(The landscape evokes feelings of stillness and deep quiet.)

"Reading poetry put her in a meditative mood."

(It brought her into a state of calm, deep, inward reflection.)
Meditative means having — or creating — the quality of deep, calm, unhurried, inward-focused thought and stillness, whether in a person, an activity, a mood, a piece of art, or a place.
10486:
Before diving into the individual meanings, here is the single idea that runs through all of them:

A medium is something that sits in the middle — between two things — and connects them, carries something between them, or balances them.

Think of it like a bridge. A bridge doesn't have value by itself — its value is that it links one side to the other. In every meaning of "medium," something is playing this bridging role. Once you understand this, every sense of the word will feel natural.

1. A Middle Point or Balanced Ground

This is the most literal, foundational sense. A medium is a point that falls between two extremes — not too much of one thing, not too much of the other.

Example: You want to save money, but you also want to enjoy life. Spending everything is one extreme; saving every single penny is the other. A medium between these two is a balanced, sensible middle ground where you do a bit of both wisely.

This is exactly what the common phrase "a happy medium" means — a satisfying compromise or balance between two opposing things.

"She didn't want the party to be too formal or too casual, so they chose a happy medium — smart but relaxed."

2. A Channel or Method of Communication

A medium (plural: media) is any system, method, or platform through which information, ideas, or art is delivered from one person (or group) to another.

Think about how you receive information and entertainment: through television, radio, newspapers, books, podcasts, the internet, social media, film. Each one of these is a medium — it is the channel through which a message travels from a sender to you, the receiver.

Examples:

  • "Television is a powerful medium for reaching millions of people at once."
  • "Before the internet, print was the dominant medium for spreading news."
  • "She chose film as her medium to tell stories about social justice."

This is the sense that gives us the word "media" — when journalists and commentators talk about "the media," they are referring to the collective body of these channels: newspapers, TV stations, online platforms, and so on.

Important distinction: The word "media" is the plural of this sense of "medium." So:

  • One channel → a medium (e.g., television)
  • Several channels → the media (e.g., television, radio, and newspapers together)

3. The Material or Substance an Artist Uses

In art, a medium (plural: media or mediums) is the specific material or method an artist employs to create their work. It is the "bridge" between the artist's idea and the finished artwork.

Examples:

  • A painter might work in the medium of oil paint, watercolour, or charcoal.
  • A sculptor might work in the medium of marble, clay, or bronze.
  • A photographer works in the medium of photography.
  • A digital artist works in the medium of digital illustration.

"Her preferred medium was watercolour because it produced a soft, flowing quality that oil paint couldn't."
"He was a sculptor who worked exclusively in the medium of recycled metal."

Note that this use also extends beyond visual art. A writer's medium is language. A filmmaker's medium is film. A musician's medium is sound.

4. A Substance Through Which Something Travels

In science, a medium (plural: media) is the material or environment through which energy, waves, or forces pass. It is the "bridge" that lets something travel from one place to another.

This sense is especially common in physics and biology.

Examples:

  • Sound needs a physical substance to travel through. Air, water, and solids are all media through which sound waves move. (In a vacuum — where there is nothing — sound cannot travel at all, because there is no medium.)
  • Light can travel through several media: air, water, glass, or even a vacuum.
  • Heat travels through solids, liquids, and gases, each acting as a medium.

"Sound travels much faster through water than through air because water is a denser medium."
"Glass is a transparent medium — light can pass through it."

In biology and medicine, a culture medium (also just called a medium) is a specially prepared substance — often a gel or liquid — in which bacteria, cells, or other microorganisms are grown in a laboratory.

"Scientists cultured the bacteria on an agar medium to observe how they grew."

5. A Person Who Claims to Communicate With Spirits

A medium (plural: mediums) is a person who claims to have the ability to act as a bridge between the living world and the world of the dead — to receive or relay messages from the spirits of deceased people.

This connects perfectly to the core idea: the medium is the go-between, the channel between two worlds.

"The grieving family visited a medium, hoping to receive a message from their late father."
"She worked as a medium, conducting séances for people who wanted to communicate with lost loved ones."

Note: Whether such abilities are real is a matter of personal belief, not scientific consensus — but the word itself is completely standard and widely used.

6. A Middle Size

In everyday commercial use, medium is used as a noun to refer to a size that falls between small and large — in clothing, drinks, food portions, and similar things.

"Do you have this jacket in a medium?"
"I ordered a medium, but they gave me a large by mistake."
The Two Plural Forms and When to Use Each

This is a common source of confusion, so it is worth being precise:

"Media" — the Latin-style plural. Used for:

  • Channels of communication (television and radio are powerful media)
  • Scientific and biological substances (culture media)
  • Artistic materials (mixed media artwork)

"Mediums" — the regular English plural. Used for:

  • Spiritual intermediaries (a group of mediums gathered for the séance)
  • Clothing/commercial sizes (we have mediums and larges in stock)
  • Sometimes artistic materials, especially in informal use

A helpful rule of thumb: if you are talking about people or sizes, use mediums. If you are talking about substances, channels, or materials, media is usually preferred — though "mediums" is increasingly accepted in everyday speech for artistic materials.

"The medium is the message" — This was coined by the thinker Marshall McLuhan. It means that the channel through which something is communicated is not just a neutral container — it actually shapes and changes the meaning and impact of the message itself.

For example: the same news story told in a newspaper, on television, and as a 30-second social media video are experienced very differently by the audience, even if the core facts are identical. The medium itself is communicating something beyond just the words.

Every single sense of "medium" as a noun comes back to the same idea:

It is something in the middle — connecting, carrying, balancing, or bridging between two sides.

Whether it is a spiritual go-between, a channel for news, a material for painting, a substance through which sound travels, or a comfortable midpoint between two extremes — it is always the thing in between that makes a connection possible.
10487:
A medley is a collection of different, varied things brought together as one. The most important quality of a medley is variety — the items in a medley are noticeably different from each other, yet they exist together under one roof, so to speak.

Think of it this way: if you grabbed one song, it's just a song. But if you grabbed five different songs and performed them back-to-back as one continuous piece, that's a medley. The variety is the whole point.
The Three Main Contexts Where "Medley" is Used

1. Music (Most Common Usage)

A medley in music is a single performance made up of several different songs played one after another, usually connected smoothly without a full stop between them. The songs typically share a theme — for example, a singer might perform a medley of love songs from the 1980s, blending one into the next.

"The orchestra performed a medley of film scores."

Key point: in a musical medley, you can still recognise each individual song — they haven't been blended into something unrecognisable. Each piece keeps its identity, but they're all stitched together into one performance.

2. Food

A medley in cooking refers to a dish made up of several different ingredients of the same category mixed together. A "vegetable medley" means a dish containing a variety of vegetables — say, carrots, broccoli, zucchini, and bell peppers — all cooked and served together.

"The chef prepared a fresh fruit medley of strawberries, mango, and kiwi."

3. Swimming (Sports)

In competitive swimming, a medley is a race that combines four different swimming strokes — butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, and freestyle — either swum one after another by a single swimmer (called the individual medley), or by four different swimmers each doing one stroke (called a medley relay).

"She won gold in the 400-metre individual medley."

Beyond music, food, and swimming, "medley" is also used in everyday language to describe any varied mixture of things. It doesn't have to be something physical — it can describe sounds, feelings, ideas, people, events, or anything else.

"The festival was filled with a medley of sounds — drums, laughter, and sizzling street food."
"His speech was a medley of jokes, serious points, and personal stories."
"The market sold a medley of goods — spices, handmade crafts, and vintage books."

In all these cases, the word signals that what you're looking at (or hearing, or experiencing) is diverse and varied, not uniform.
What Makes a Medley Different from Similar Words?

This is where precision matters. Several words seem similar to "medley" but they're not quite the same.

Medley vs. Mixture — A "mixture" is a broad, general word for anything combined. A medley is more specific: it implies noticeable variety between the parts, and it's often used in more deliberate, curated contexts (music, cooking, sports). You wouldn't call a medley of songs a "mixture of songs" — it would sound odd.

Medley vs. Blend — In a blend, the individual components lose their separate identity and merge into something new (think of a smoothie — you can't pull the mango back out). In a medley, the individual parts remain recognisable. A medley of songs still lets you hear each song; a vegetable medley still lets you see each vegetable.

Medley vs. Assortment — An "assortment" simply means a group of various things. A medley carries a slightly more intentional, curated feeling — as though the varied things have been brought together with a purpose, especially in creative or culinary contexts.

Medley vs. Hodgepodge / Mishmash — These words suggest messy, random, or chaotic variety. A medley, by contrast, has a neutral to positive tone. It suggests rich, enjoyable variety rather than disorder.

"Medley" is generally a positive or neutral word. It celebrates variety rather than criticising it. When someone calls something a medley, they're usually not complaining — they're pointing out that you're getting a rich, diverse experience.

It also often implies that the variety is enjoyable or interesting. A street described as having "a medley of smells" paints a vivid, lively picture of that place.

If you want one simple image to remember "medley" forever:

Think of a DJ's set at a party — they play one song, then smoothly transition to another, then another, from different genres and eras, all in one continuous flow. That whole set is a medley. Different things. One experience. Variety is the point.

That's medley.
10488:
A meed is a deserved reward or recompense — something given to a person in return for their service, effort, or merit. Think of it as "what you rightfully get for what you did."

The heart of this word is the idea of deservingness. A meed isn't just any gift or payment. It carries the sense of a return that is fitting and proportional — the right recognition for the right action.

If someone works hard, fights bravely, serves loyally, or achieves something worthy, the honor, payment, or recognition they receive in return is their meed. It's their due. Their just reward.

You can think of it through this simple lens:

Action → Meed (the fitting return for that action)

A soldier's meed might be glory or honor after a battle. A servant's meed might be payment after loyal service. A poet's meed might be the praise of readers after a great work.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

The word carries a sense of justice and proportion. It doesn't mean an arbitrary or accidental reward. It means something owed — something the person has earned and deserves to receive.

In most uses, meed has a positive or neutral flavor — a well-earned reward, deserved recognition, fitting praise. But occasionally, in older texts, it can also refer to a deserved consequence in a broader sense, meaning whatever outcome properly corresponds to one's deeds (though this is rarer).
Register: When and Where You'll See This Word

Meed is an archaic word. You will almost never hear it in everyday modern English conversation. It belongs to the world of:

  • Classical English poetry (Shakespeare, Spenser, Milton, Keats)
  • Older literary prose
  • Formal or deliberately elevated writing that reaches back to an older style

When you come across it in these contexts, it is almost always a conscious stylistic choice — the writer is invoking a formal, noble, slightly old-world quality. The word has a ceremonial gravity to it.

Here are some clear examples to solidify the meaning:

  1. "After decades of faithful service, she finally received her meed of recognition."
    → She finally got the acknowledgment she had long deserved.
  2. "The warrior asked for no treasure — his meed was the honor of victory alone."
    → His deserved reward was simply the glory of winning.
  3. "Let every man receive his meed according to his deeds."
    → Let every person get what they rightfully deserve based on what they've done.
  4. "Praise is a poor meed for such extraordinary sacrifice."
    → Mere praise is an insufficient reward for so great a sacrifice.

If you want one clean mental anchor for this word:

Meed = a deserved reward; what someone has rightfully earned.

It sits in the same family of meaning as recompense, due, reward, and desert (as in "just deserts"). But meed is the most literary and archaic of these, and carries the strongest sense of something being precisely fitting — not too much, not too little, but exactly what was earned.

To further sharpen your understanding, here are words that overlap closely in meaning:

  • Recompense — something given in return for effort or loss (more neutral, modern)
  • Due — what someone rightfully deserves ("he got his due")
  • Desert — in the phrase just deserts, meaning deserved outcome
  • Reward — the broader, everyday version of this idea

Among all these, meed is the most poetic and archaic, with the strongest literary flavor. When a writer uses meed instead of simply reward, they are deliberately reaching for elevation and formality.
10489:
Meek describes a person who is quiet, gentle, and unlikely to argue, fight back, or stand up for themselves — even when they have a perfectly good reason to. A meek person tends to accept things without resistance, go along with what others want, and stay silent when others might speak up. Not necessarily because they agree or are happy, but because they don't push themselves forward.

A simple picture: if someone treats a meek person unfairly, they won't loudly demand better. If someone insults them, they won't snap back. They absorb it, stay quiet, and move on.

This word has two faces depending on where and how it's used.

The positive side comes mostly from a spiritual and moral tradition. The famous phrase "The meek shall inherit the earth" (from the Bible's Sermon on the Mount) uses meek to mean humble, gentle, and patient — the opposite of arrogant, aggressive, or power-hungry. In this light, being meek is a strength. It means you're peaceful and restrained even when you could choose to dominate. You don't throw your weight around. You don't brag. You don't force your will on others. This kind of meekness is deeply admired in many spiritual and ethical traditions.

The negative side is how the word is more commonly used in everyday modern life. Here, calling someone meek usually suggests they are too passive — so gentle that they let people walk all over them, so reluctant to push back that they can't advocate for themselves. In this sense, meekness looks less like humility and more like a lack of courage or confidence. If your manager says, "She's a bit meek for this role," they mean she seems too timid to handle pressure, conflict, or leadership demands.

So the word carries a slight tension: it can describe admirable gentleness or a problematic lack of assertiveness, depending on the context and the speaker's tone.

A meek person tends to speak softly and hesitantly. They rarely say no to requests, even unreasonable ones. They avoid conflict almost at any cost. They don't demand things — even things they're owed. There's often something physically small or withdrawn about how they carry themselves: a downward gaze, a quiet voice, a posture that doesn't take up much space.

Importantly, the word can describe a momentary behavior as well as a personality trait. You don't have to be a meek person to do something meekly. For example:

  • He gave a meek apology. (It was soft and unconvincing — he said sorry without real force or sincerity.)
  • She raised a meek protest. (She objected, but so gently that no one really took it seriously.)
  • He accepted the criticism with a meek nod. (He didn't argue — just quietly accepted it.)

In these cases, "meek" colors a specific act: it tells you the action was done without confidence, force, or assertiveness.
How Meek Differs from Similar Words

Shy is about social anxiety — a shy person wants to speak or engage but feels nervous doing so. Meek is more about submission — a meek person may not even try to push back, not out of nervousness, but out of a pattern of yielding.

Humble means having a modest, grounded view of yourself — not boasting or acting superior. Meek overlaps with this but goes further: humility is about not inflating yourself, while meekness is about not defending yourself either.

Timid is very close to meek but leans more toward fear. A timid person holds back because they're afraid. A meek person holds back because submission is simply their nature or their choice. The two often go together, but they're not identical.

Docile means easy to manage or control, readily obedient — it's often used for animals. Meek carries a more human weight and often implies a moral or emotional dimension that "docile" doesn't.

Meekly (adverb): Describes how something is done — quietly, gently, without resistance.
"She meekly agreed to stay late, even though she already had plans."

Meekness (noun): The quality or state of being meek.
"His meekness made it easy for others to take advantage of him."

"Meek as a lamb" — This phrase means someone is extremely gentle and non-threatening, calm and harmless like a young sheep. It emphasizes total softness and submissiveness, usually with a touch of affection or pity.

Meek always means the same thing: quietly gentle, yielding, and unlikely to assert or defend oneself forcefully. What changes is the judgment attached to it. In a world that admires humility and peacefulness, meekness is a virtue. In a world that rewards confidence and assertiveness, meekness can look like weakness.

A truly meek person isn't angry or cold — they're soft. They're the ones who quietly accept more than their share, who say "it's fine" when it isn't, who would rather keep the peace than win an argument. Whether that's noble or naïve depends entirely on the situation you're looking at.
